articles.excerpt: Candy was recalled in 13 states, including Ohio and Indiana, due to an undeclared allergen.

CINCINNATI (WKRC) - Candy was recalled in 13 states, including Ohio and Indiana, due to an undeclared allergen.

According to a recall report from the Food and Drug Administration, bags of "Chocolately Eyeballs" sold under the Crystal Temptations brand at Marshalls, TJ Maxx, Homegoods, and Sierra Trading Post were recalled because their packaging did not declare the presence of milk in the product.

The candies were recalled in Arizona, Texas, Virginia, Georgia, Massachusetts, North Carolina, Indiana, Nevada, California, New Jersey, Connecticut, Ohio, and Wyoming.

The products affected by the recall were:

Customers were advised to "destroy the product" and the report advised that refunds would not be available at the point of sale. Instead, customers were told to contact Crystal Temptations with proof of purchase for a refund.

articles.title: I Love to Read: World’s top creator and bestselling author release high-stakes thriller
articles.excerpt: MrBeast and James Patterson launch their global thriller 'The Most Dangerous Games' today, featuring a high-stakes $1 billion contest.
articles.content:
INDIANAPOLIS (WISH) — YouTube creator MrBeast and bestselling author James Patterson have teamed up for a new thriller that combines high-stakes competition with a fight for humanity’s survival.

“The Most Dangerous Games” launches globally Sept. 1, 2026.

The novel follows 100 contestants competing in a secretive competition with a $1 billion prize. As the games unfold, the stakes go beyond winning, with the fate of humanity tied to the outcome.

The book brings together the world of MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, and Patterson’s decades of experience writing bestselling thrillers.

Donaldson is known for large-scale challenges, elaborate competitions and philanthropy campaigns. He also founded Beast Industries and operates one of the most-subscribed individual channels on YouTube.

Patterson is the author of hundreds of books and has received numerous honors, including an Edgar Award, 10 Emmy Awards, the Literarian Award and the National Humanities Medal.

The two discussed the collaboration during a virtual event Aug. 13, highlighting how Donaldson’s experience with competition and entertainment influenced the story while Patterson brought his thriller-writing expertise to the project.

HarperCollins acquired the rights to the book and is distributing it worldwide.

“The Most Dangerous Games” is available in standard, deluxe limited and digital editions through major retailers.More information can be found here.

articles.title: Under Trump, the IRS’ audit revenue falls in predictable and damaging ways
articles.excerpt: Following sweeping cuts, the tax agency brought in 35% less last year than the year before, and there’s no great mystery as to why.
articles.content:
Donald Trump’s second term has been a difficult one for the IRS. The tax agency has struggled with resignations, DOGE-imposed disruptions and the abandonment of a much-needed modernization initiative.

Complicating matters, there’s been a revolving door at the IRS administrator’s office. In the first seven months of Trump’s second term, seven different people led the agency. The eighth was Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who already had another important full-time job. Since March, no one has served as IRS commissioner, although the White House tapped Frank Bisignano to serve as the agency’s chief executive officer (an office that’s never existed before), despite the fact that he also has a full-time job running the Social Security Administration.

With all of this tumult, it’s tempting to ask how the IRS can be expected to fulfill its core functions. The answer to that question is that it’s not completing some of its core functions. The New York Times reported:

articles.title: WARDOGS Devs Explain Why The FPS Games Show Is Here: 'This Is Not Worth It'
articles.excerpt: At Gamescom, I caught up with BULKHEAD, the studio behind WARDOGS, to talk about the new broadcast, The FPS Games Show.
articles.content:
At Gamescom, I was lucky enough to sit down with BULKHEAD to discuss the upcoming early access release of WARDOGS, easily one of the most highly anticipated first-person shooters coming to the market in the very near future. I caught up with CEO Joe Brammer and CFO Mark Pinney, but before we started talking about their game, I wanted to learn more about The FPS Games Show.

On September 3, The FPS Games Show debuts worldwide, with a stellar line-up of first-person shooter games (and some special guests) presenting new trailers, upcoming content, and big changes. It’s a brand-new offering in the showcase space, and I just had to ask Brammer and Pinney why BULKHEAD was leading the charge by producing the entire broadcast.

Traditional Gaming Shows Aren’t Worth The Cost

In case you’re out of the loop in the gaming space, there are more than a few showcases that take place every year. The largest ones, such as Summer Game Fest, Gamescom’s Opening Night Live ceremony, and The Game Awards, pull in millions of viewers.

But they also cost extortionate amounts to get your game seen.

RELATED: WARDOGS Devs Talk Monetization

In some cases, we’ve heard of developers or publishers paying hundreds of thousands of dollars for spots in these showcases, pricing out the little guy and decimating marketing budgets for a minute or so of airtime.

That’s the cost of advertising, but it can feel extremely unfair. It’s why we at Insider Gaming hosted our showcase in May to promote a slew of incredible indie games for free, all of which were looking for funding or a publisher.

Now, BULKHEAD, the studio behind WARDOGS, an upcoming, large-scale shooter, is hosting The FPS Games Show, another free-to-access broadcast focusing specifically on the first-person space. It boasts some huge names in the lineup, including Gray Zone Warfare, Rainbow Six Siege, Escape from Tarkov, and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam.

But I was eager to learn about the intricacies of the show, so I asked Brammer and Pinney, the core of the leadership team at BULKHEAD, why they felt the need to assemble and produce the showcase, and why now was the right time to present it.

Brammer dived in first:

Our specialty is FPS games, and when we were trying to market out game, when we were trying to get out there, we talked to quite a few different, big shows, trying to get a spot on them.

We can do it, but they’re asking for ’50k’ for you know, a minute? And you think, ‘Maybe that’s worth it.’ And then they’ll go up as far as 300, 400, 500k, and we’re like, ‘That isn’t worth it.’

When you speak to some of the bigger guys, the big studios, they’re saying the same thing: ‘This is not worth it.’ Especially when it comes to FPS games.

We can do it, but they’re asking for ’50k’ for you know, a minute? And you think, ‘Maybe that’s worth it.’ And then they’ll go up as far as 300, 400, 500k, and we’re like, ‘That isn’t worth it.’

When you speak to some of the bigger guys, the big studios, they’re saying the same thing: ‘This is not worth it.’ Especially when it comes to FPS games.

But Brammer then expanded, explaining how it’s not just the cost of getting a slot on these shows that’s the problem. It’s how irrelevant that slot might be. Typically, these broadcasts are diverse, presenting an array of titles that try to appeal to as many people as possible, but that can result in some confusing, convoluted streams packed with all kinds of genres.

That’s what Brammer was talking about:

You’re on a stream next to an Asian MMO, and then XBOX’s new single-player game, and it doesn’t really translate to sales, promotion, getting people looking at your game properly – the right people looking at your game.

It just wasn’t worth it, it felt like to me.

We have, as developers, felt quite taken advantage of by the industry for a long time. The fact that there are people and big companies (and individuals) taking huge chunks of money off us, just trying to create the very thing the industry revolves around… It felt a bit like… ‘This is bulls***.’

It just wasn’t worth it, it felt like to me.

We have, as developers, felt quite taken advantage of by the industry for a long time. The fact that there are people and big companies (and individuals) taking huge chunks of money off us, just trying to create the very thing the industry revolves around… It felt a bit like… ‘This is bulls***.’

BULKHEAD then decided to send out feelers, see who would be interested in setting up an entirely new showcase to represent only first-person shooter games, and the response was, by all accounts, entirely unexpected.

RELATED: WARDOGS Could Get an Extraction Mode

Before long, some of the most important players in the genre had thrown their hat in the wrong, enticed by the notion that this broadcast is entirely free for developers to take part in.

Pinney, the company’s CFO, explained why BULKHEAD had pioneered The FPS Games Show:

Especially now, recently being independent, our philosophy is quite forward-thinking. We don’t like the norms of how games have been made or developed or how marketing happens.

We’re always looking for ways to improve how it works. I think you just need a leader to do it.

That shows not only in The FPS Games Show and how we’re marketing it but in the game itself, as well.

The FPS Games Show is set to broadcast on September 3 at 7 PM UK Time, and it has one hell of a lineup. Let us know on the Insider Gaming Discord server if you’ll be checking out the stream, and check back after the event, because we’ll have a full breakdown of everything revealed.

For more Insider Gaming coverage, check out the news that the Savvy Games Group CEO has stepped down. Also, don’t forget to sign up for our weekly newsletter

articles.title: Cyrus Allen provides Chiefs fans a glimpse into the respect Patrick Mahomes demands
articles.excerpt: The Kansas City Chiefs are uber-excited about Cyrus Allen, who, in turn, pointed out how exciting it is to work alongside Super Bowl MVP Patrick Mahomes.
articles.content:
There has been an undeniable level of disrespect swirling around the Kansas City Chiefs and Patrick Mahomes after a rough 2025 season. It's as if one year of failure gave permission for league pundits and fans to get every wrong take off their chest when it comes to Mahomes and KC. Underrating Mahomes is a dangerous decision, one that fellow players clearly don't make the mistake of doing.

Fifth-round rookie and training camp darling, Cyrus Allen is the latest example of how Mahomes has continued to demand respect and inspire his teammates despite the quarterback's lessened numbers over the last three regular seasons.

In last year's injury-shortened season, Mahomes finished with 3,587 passing yards and 22 passing touchdowns. These are good numbers in a full season for nearly half the league; only by the lofty standards the three-time Super Bowl MVP has established would this be an invitation to cast doubt and rank less accomplished players ahead of him.

Gabriela Hernandez of KWCH10 News provided a glimpse of the respect Mahomes still garners. "I'm still lookin' at Pat like, 'Damn, this Patrick Mahomes I'm around...," Allen said postgame after a preseason loss. This points to the undeniable legend who has a young player starstruck. It serves as a reminder of who Mahomes is, no matter the recent numbers.

Kansas City's fifth-round rookie and training camp darling was starstruck playing alongside the three-time Super Bowl MVP

There is still no one in the league who can compare their resume to that of Mahomes and have a fair argument. There is already a valid argument to be made that the signal-caller is only behind Tom Brady when having the GOAT conversation.

It is important to remember that recent seasons have seen numbers decline based not on ability, but on the cast around the quarterback as well as playcalling. The lack of investment in the receiver room since Tyreek Hill left exposes just how much Kansas City has grown to rely on Mahomes. It seems the Chiefs have simply believed that anything close to a capable offensive line will be more than enough to provide the Chiefs a chance to make a Super Bowl run.

This cannot be denied when you consider the past two groups of receivers that Mahomes has taken to a Super Bowl. In fact, the majority of the Chiefs' wide receiver room during the 2023 season is now out of the league. Patrick Mahomes dragged those dudes to a Super Bowl victory.

articles.title: NFL Execs, Coaches Identify 10 Breakout Players to Watch in 2026
articles.excerpt: More than a dozen sources weigh in on first- and second-year players, including a pair of top pass rushers and a second-year wideout.
articles.content:
In this story:

Every year, there are a handful of young stars who swing the NFL season. Last year, rookie defensive back Nick Emmanwori of the Seahawks was a prime example. In 2024, corners Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean helped the Eagles win their second Super Bowl as rookie starters. In 2023, rookie receiver Rashee Rice and second-year corners Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson helped the Chiefs confirm their dynasty. 

Of course, not all great performances come in a championship season. Most don’t. In 2025, we saw myriad fantastic campaigns from first-year talents, including Colston Loveland and Luther Burden III in Chicago, Tyler Warren with the Colts and James Pearce Jr. for the Falcons, just to name a few. 

This summer, I traveled around the East Coast as part of my training camp tour for Sports Illustrated and noted the best rookies I watched. I also reached out to more than a dozen sources on coaching staffs and in front offices to get their opinions on first- and second-year players who they believe are set to have breakout seasons. 

Here’s the list of 10 names to earmark, starting with one in Gotham.

David Bailey, DE, Jets

Bailey was taken No. 2 by the Jets, who selected him over other options, including linebackers Arvell Reese and Sonny Styles. The move was risky for general manager Darren Mougey, but early returns say he won’t regret it. 

During a joint practice with the Buccaneers, Bailey was so dominant in one-on-one reps that right tackle Luke Goedeke got into a fight with him. They got into another skirmish, again mostly because Bailey kept winning his reps. 

Goedeke shouldn’t feel bad. Coming out of Texas Tech, where he led the nation in 2025 with 14.5 sacks and 19.5 tackles for loss, Bailey has looked the part of a top draft pick. Against Pittsburgh, Bailey grabbed his first sack, while recording two tackles throughout the preseason. 

Rueben Bain Jr., DE, Buccaneers

Bain has spent most of August putting offenses on notice. Bain, who was maligned throughout the draft process for his 30⅞-inch arms, is showing he might be an outlier to a normal rule decreeing pass rushers need to have more length. 

Against the Chiefs in Tampa Bay’s second preseason game, Bain showed his power, using an inside “hump” move to put right tackle Kahlil Benson on skates. It reminded fans of his Miami days, where he recorded 9.5 sacks as a junior. In that aforementioned joint practice with the Jets, Bain was routinely in the backfield during both individual and team drills.

Currently dealing with a sprained MCL, Bain is projected to start on one edge with YaYa Diaby and Al-Quadin Muhammad rotating in on the other. 

Josh Cameron, WR, Jaguars

Cameron is an intriguing name, and one that has flown under the national radar with the Jaguars having better-known receivers, including Jakobi Meyers, Parker Washington and Brian Thomas Jr. 

Still, the sixth-round pick from Baylor has turned heads in Jacksonville’s facility. While Cameron will likely start as a special teams contributor who can rotate in offensively, the 23-year-old is a big-bodied target at 6'1" and 223 pounds with the ability to wall off defenders, particularly in the red zone. At Baylor, Cameron had 121 catches for 1,626 yards and 19 touchdowns over his past two seasons. 

At times this summer, Cameron ran with the first team when Thomas and Meyers were nursing injuries and performed well. Should Jacksonville need to reach into its depth during the season, the rookie might have his name called after an impressive camp.

Charles Demmings, CB, Vikings

The Vikings are looking for players who can help in the secondary. Talking to people in the building, they may have found one in Demmings. 

A fifth-round rookie from SF Austin, Demmings has shown potential in the early going. While he’s not projected to start with veteran Isaiah Rodgers ahead of him, Demmings could emerge into a larger role as he gains more trust. At 6'1" and 193 pounds, Demmings can play the physical brand of man-to-man football that coordinator Brian Flores loves, something that showed up throughout camp. 

With Minnesota trying to find stability at the position, both in the short and long term, Demmings is a player to watch moving forward.

Kaleb Elarms-Orr, ILB, Bills

In Buffalo, the talk has been about the new coaching staff led by Joe Brady and an offense infused by veteran receiver DJ Moore. But the other story at camp was Elarms-Orr, a fourth-round rookie trying to force his way into the linebacker rotation.

As a senior with the Horned Frogs, Elarms-Orr posted 110 tackles, including 11 for loss and four sacks. Throughout his first few months with the Bills, the 23-year-old continued to show flashes of a productive pro while primarily playing on the second team. Still, expect the rookie to earn time in coordinator Jim Leonhard’s 3–4 scheme, likely getting snaps in a rotation with Terrel Bernard and Dorian Williams. 

In the preseason, Elarms-Orr was relatively quiet with only three tackles, but after enjoying a productive summer, the TCU product should be on your radar.

Matthew Golden, WR, Packers

The first non-rookie on our list, the Packers are giving rave reviews of their 2025 first-round selection. 

This offseason, Green Bay remade the receiver room by trading Dontayvion Wicks and allowing Romeo Doubs to leave for the Patriots in free agency. They did so because they believed in their other options, including Jayden Reed, Christian Watson and Golden, the latter of whom posted only 29 catches on 44 targets for 361 yards and zero touchdowns in his first year. 

Now poised for a bigger role, Golden has been one of Green Bay’s standouts in camp. With running back Josh Jacobs on the commissioner’s exempt list, the Packers are likely to throw even more than normal, giving Golden plenty of chances to show his improvements from a year ago.

Romello Height, DE, 49ers

Height, the No. 70 pick in April, took the long road to reach the NFL. In college, the defensive end spent time over six years at Auburn, USC, Georgia Tech and Texas Tech, playing in 50 games and amassing 16.5 sacks. 

Now at 25 years old, the Niners believe he can be an impact player, even if the preseason numbers haven’t been impressive. Considering he’s been dealing with an ankle injury throughout much of August, he hasn’t been able to showcase his best. He’ll have an immediate opportunity in Week 1 when the 49ers take on the Super Bowl-favorite Rams in Australia on Thursday night of the opening week.

If things go well, both on a healthy and production front, San Francisco is hoping Height becomes a complement to Joey Bosa and Osa Odighizuwa on the line, helping the Niners improve on what was a league-worst 20 sacks. 

Anthony Hill Jr., LB, Titans

Hill has been all over the field for former 49ers defensive coordinator Robert Saleh in Tennessee.

A second-round pick out of Texas, Hill has shined. In the Titans’ final preseason game against the Bears, he was asked to play inside linebacker and repeatedly flashed, totaling a team-high six tackles, including five solos. For the preseason, Hill recorded 13 tackles and an interception coming off a collegiate career that included 31.5 tackles for loss and 17 sacks over three seasons.

With the Titans completely revamping their roster, Hill projects to be a long-term answer while competing for snaps against veterans Cedric Gray and Cody Barton. While Gray is a budding star and Barton is a steady, experienced tackler, Hill’s upside will make it tough to keep the former Longhorns star off the field. 

Ja’Kobi Lane, WR, Ravens

Few, if any, rookies have enjoyed more hype this summer than Lane, who comes in from USC to give Lamar Jackson another weapon in Baltimore’s passing attack.

With Zay Flowers and little else on the perimeter to be excited about in recent years, the Ravens might have struck gold with their third-rounder. Lane has impressed throughout the offseason, and this summer caught four passes for 47 yards and a touchdown, including 38 yards with a score against the Eagles in the preseason opener. 

At 6'4" and 200 pounds, Lane can sky for the ball while making acrobatic catches, something he’s done repeatedly in training camp. When I was in Baltimore to watch a joint practice between the Ravens and Commanders, Lane ran with the first team (Flowers didn’t participate that day) and looked the part, consistently running crisp routes to gain separation. 

If Lane develops into a weapon for Jackson, the trajectory of the offense could change under new coordinator Declan Doyle.

R Mason Thomas, DE, Chiefs

With the No. 40 pick, the Chiefs did something they never do: draft a small edge rusher. 

Thomas, who weighs 239 pounds, is about 25-30 pounds lighter than the defensive ends coordinator Steve Spagnuolo has employed in Kansas City, including Frank Clark, Carlos Dunlap and George Karlaftis. However, early results say the Chiefs should have considered this path much sooner. 

Thomas has been destructive throughout the preseason. In three games, he’s racked up four tackles, three quarterback hits, two passes defensed and a sack. It’s early, but the Chiefs believe they may have found someone who can push the pocket and create havoc from the opposite side of Karlaftis, with perennial All-Pro Chris Jones working on the interior. 

While Kansas City is typically hesitant to start rookies over veterans, look for Thomas and fellow rookie corner Mansoor Delane to buck that trend.

Matt Verderame is a national NFL staff writer for Sports Illustrated, writing features, columns and more. Before joining Sports Illustrated in March 2023, Verderame wrote for FanSided and SB Nation. He’s a proud husband to Stephanie and father of two girls, Maisy and Genevieve. In his spare time, Verderame is an avid collector of vintage baseball cards.

articles.title: Is MrBeast and James Patterson’s Novel Collaboration Headed for a Disastrous Debut?
articles.excerpt: MrBeast and James Patterson's snew novel collaboration, The Most Dangerous Games, has been tracking poorly in presales, according to a report.
articles.content:
As of last week, preorders for 'The Most Dangerous Games' were reportedly "numbering in the four digits." But sources insist the authors are on track.

Could MrBeast and James Patterson have a dud on their hands?

According to Semafor, the pair’s new novel collaboration, titled The Most Dangerous Games, has been tracking poorly in presales.

Citing anonymous sources “close to the project,” Semafor reported that the thriller is “on track to be a historic bomb.” As of last week, preorders were “numbering in the four digits … a tiny fraction of what the publisher will need to justify Patterson’s and YouTuber Jimmy Donaldson’s [aka MrBeast] hefty fees.” As of Monday, the book was at No. 18 on Amazon’s new releases list.

However, another knowledgeable source told The Hollywood Reporter that the number of preorders is not unusual, particularly for a genre novel, and that what really matters is first-week sales. They also pointed out that the book is currently at No. 1 on the mystery novels list.

The Hollywood Reporter has reached out to reps for book publisher HarperCollins for comment.

According to the book’s webpage, the logline is: “A thousand strangers receive the invitation. One hundred make the cut. An unprecedented competition from MrBeast, the world’s #1 creator with more than a billion followers, and James Patterson, the world’s #1 bestselling author, where the stakes couldn’t be higher.

“The Games begin in Antarctica, where one wrong step “on the ice kills you, and they never let up: Shark water off a remote Chilean island, desert heat that cooks you where you stand, storm-battered peaks, and caves so black you cannot find your own hand. No rescue. No second chances. A billion dollars to whoever is still standing.

“Then the terrain stops being the thing that can kill you, and the other players start. Alliances turn into ambushes. Trust becomes the sharpest weapon. And somewhere above it all, a hidden voice is watching every move, testing, deciding who deserves to survive.”

Donaldson and Patterson have been promoting the book on social media, including in a YouTube short titled “Read My Book, You Could Win $1,000,000.” Donaldson, who has 515 million subscribers on YouTube, is known for giving away money to his followers for taking part in (and successfully completing) various outlandish stunts.
